title: Νόστος σὺν ἵπποις
titleEn: The Return with the Horses — Iliad 10.482–579
about: Athena puts might into Diomedes, who kills Thracians as a lion falls on unguarded sheep while Odysseus drags the bodies clear so the horses will not shy. Diomedes takes the king as the thirteenth, and Odysseus ties up and leads out the king's horses, striking them with his bow because he forgot the whip. As Diomedes wonders whether to haul off the chariot or kill more, Athena tells him to go back before another god rouses the Trojans. They ride off, Apollo wakes the Thracian cousin Hippocoon, and he wails at the sight of the dead. At the ships Nestor hears hoofbeats and guesses at the riders; when they arrive he asks how they won such horses, and Odysseus credits the gods and tells of the king, the twelve, and the scout. They tie the horses beside Diomedes' own, set Dolon's spoils in the ship for Athena, wash off the sweat in the sea, bathe, eat, and pour her a libation of honey-sweet wine.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἔμπνευσε μένος γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and in him breathed might gleaming-eyed Athena,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and gleaming-eyed Athena breathed might into Diomedes,
sentences.n: The speaker is Odysseus, ending his appeal of 477–481, and τῷ ‘in him’ is Diomedes, who has just been told to put forth his might. ἔμπνευσε is the aorist of ἐμπνέω ‘breathe into’: a god puts μένος ‘might’ into a hero before a fight. φάτο is unaugmented (Attic ἔφατο), and γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ is the house rendering of Athena’s stock epithet.

sentences.t: κτεῖνε δ’ ἐπιστροφάδην·
sentences.l: and he killed, turning this way and that;
sentences.i: and he killed them, turning this way and that;
sentences.n: Diomedes is the subject, carried over from τῷ. κτεῖνε is the unaugmented imperfect of κτείνω ‘kill’, so the killing goes on. ἐπιστροφάδην is an adverb built on ἐπιστρέφω ‘turn about’; ‘turning this way and that’ is the usual explanation, and the word is rare. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὲ στόνος ὄρνυτ’ ἀεικὴς
ἄορι θεινομένων,
sentences.l:
and of them a groaning arose, unseemly,
of them being struck with the sword,
sentences.i: and an unseemly groaning rose from them as they were struck down by the sword,
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of them’ and θεινομένων ‘being struck’ are both genitive and hang on στόνος ‘groaning’: the groaning of the men being struck. ὄρνυτ’ is ὄρνυτο, unaugmented, ‘arose’. ἀεικής ‘unseemly’ is the house rendering, and ἄορι is the dative of ἄορ ‘sword’, the means. The men struck are the sleeping Thracians of 471.

sentences.t: ἐρυθαίνετο δ’ αἵματι γαῖα.
sentences.l: and was reddened with blood the earth.
sentences.i: and the earth was reddened with blood.
sentences.n: ἐρυθαίνετο is the imperfect passive of ἐρυθαίνω ‘make red’, a rare verb built on ἐρυθρός ‘red’. αἵματι is the dative of αἷμα ‘blood’, the means, and γαῖα ‘earth’ is the subject, held to the end.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ λέων μήλοισιν ἀσημάντοισιν ἐπελθὼν
αἴγεσιν ἢ ὀΐεσσι κακὰ φρονέων ἐνορούσῃ,
sentences.l:
And as a lion, upon flocks unguarded having come,
upon goats or sheep with evil in mind leaps,
sentences.i: As a lion comes upon unguarded flocks, goats or sheep, and leaps on them with evil in mind,
sentences.n: A simile begins; ὡς δέ here ‘as’ is answered by ὣς μέν ‘so’ in 487. ἐπελθών is the aorist participle ‘having come upon’, and ἐνορούσῃ the aorist subjunctive of ἐνορούω ‘leap upon’, with no ἄν, as often in similes. μήλοισιν ‘flocks’ is made exact by αἴγεσιν ἢ ὀΐεσσι ‘goats or sheep’ (datives). ἀσημάντοισιν is literally ‘unmarked’ or ‘without a sign’; the usual explanation is ‘with no herdsman’, so ‘unguarded’, but the exact sense is not certain. κακὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking evils’.

sentences.t:
ὣς μὲν Θρήϊκας ἄνδρας ἐπῴχετο Τυδέος υἱὸς
ὄφρα δυώδεκ’ ἔπεφνεν·
sentences.l:
so upon the Thracian men went the son of Tydeus
until twelve he had slain;
sentences.i: so the son of Tydeus went at the Thracian men until he had killed twelve of them;
sentences.n: ὣς μέν completes the comparison, and Τυδέος υἱός ‘son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes. ἐπῴχετο is the imperfect of ἐποίχομαι ‘go against’, with its augment inside the verb, and Θρήϊκας is the epic accusative of Θρῇξ ‘Thracian’. ὄφρα with the aorist ἔπεφνεν (an old aorist of φένω ‘slay’) is ‘until he had killed’, and δυώδεκ’ is δυώδεκα ‘twelve’. The unit stops at the raised dot, mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεὺς
ὅν τινα Τυδεΐδης ἄορι πλήξειε παραστὰς
τὸν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς μετόπισθε λαβὼν ποδὸς ἐξερύσασκε,
sentences.l:
but many-wiled Odysseus,
whichever man the Tydeus’-son struck with the sword, standing beside him,
him Odysseus from behind, taking by the foot, would drag out,
sentences.i: while Odysseus of many wiles, whenever the son of Tydeus struck a man down with his sword as he stood beside him, would take that man by the foot from behind and drag him out,
sentences.n: The sentence begins with Odysseus as subject, then starts again with a relative clause and τὸν δ’ Ὀδυσεύς; the poet puts both men in the picture at once. ὅν τινα … πλήξειε is an optative of repeated action, ‘whichever man he struck’, answered by ἐξερύσασκε, where -σκε marks the repetition: ‘would drag out’, each time. παραστάς is the aorist participle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’, μετόπισθε ‘from behind’, and ποδός a genitive of the part taken hold of. πολύμητις is ‘of many wiles’; Ὀδυσσεύς has -σσ- in 488 and Ὀδυσεύς one σ in 490, for the metre.

sentences.t:
τὰ φρονέων κατὰ θυμὸν ὅπως καλλίτριχες ἵπποι
ῥεῖα διέλθοιεν μηδὲ τρομεοίατο θυμῷ
νεκροῖς ἀμβαίνοντες·
sentences.i: with this in mind in his heart, that the fair-maned horses might pass through easily and not tremble in spirit as they stepped on corpses;
sentences.n: This is Odysseus’ purpose, and the horses are Rhesus’ team, which he is leading out. τὰ φρονέων ‘planning these things’ points forward to the ὅπως clause, whose optatives διέλθοιεν ‘might pass through’ and τρομεοίατο ‘might tremble’ make a purpose clause, ‘so that … might’. καλλίτριχες ‘fair-maned’ is the house rendering; μηδέ is ‘and not’. ἀμβαίνοντες is ἀναβαίνοντες ‘stepping up on’, with the dative νεκροῖς ‘corpses’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ἀήθεσσον γὰρ ἔτ’ αὐτῶν.
sentences.l: for they were still unused to them.
sentences.i: for they were still unused to them.
sentences.n: This gives the reason for Odysseus’ care: horses not used to corpses may shy. ἀήθεσσον is an imperfect of the verb ‘be unused to’ (ἀηθέω), in its epic form with -εσσον, and takes the genitive αὐτῶν ‘to them’ (the corpses). ἔτ’ is ‘still, as yet’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ βασιλῆα κιχήσατο Τυδέος υἱός,
sentences.l: But when indeed the king he came upon, the son of Tydeus,
sentences.i: But when the son of Tydeus came upon the king,
sentences.n: The king is Rhesus (named at 435 and 474, but not here). κιχήσατο is the aorist middle of κιχάνω ‘reach, come upon’, and Τυδέος υἱός ‘son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes. ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή marks the turn from the twelve to the king.

sentences.t:
τὸν τρισκαιδέκατον μελιηδέα θυμὸν ἀπηύρα
ἀσθμαίνοντα·
sentences.l:
him, as the thirteenth, of his honey-sweet life he deprived,
gasping;
sentences.i: he took the honey-sweet life from him, the thirteenth, as he lay gasping;
sentences.n: ἀπηύρα is the aorist of ἀπαυράω ‘take from’, with two accusatives, the man (τὸν … ἀσθμαίνοντα ‘him gasping’) and the thing taken (θυμόν). τρισκαιδέκατον ‘thirteenth’ makes the king the thirteenth victim after the twelve of 488. μελιηδέα ‘honey-sweet’ is the house rendering, and θυμός of the life that leaves the body is ‘life’. The unit stops at the raised dot, mid-line.

sentences.t:
κακὸν γὰρ ὄναρ κεφαλῆφιν ἐπέστη
τὴν νύκτ’ Οἰνεΐδαο πάϊς διὰ μῆτιν Ἀθήνης.
sentences.l:
for an evil dream stood at his head
that night, the child of Oeneus’ son, through the cunning of Athena.
sentences.i: for that night an evil dream stood at his head, the child of Oeneus’ son, by the cunning of Athena.
sentences.n: This explains the king’s gasping. ὄναρ is ‘dream’, and κεφαλῆφιν has the old ending -φιν, ‘at his head’. τὴν νύκτ’ ‘that night’ is an accusative of time. Οἰνεΐδαο is the genitive of Οἰνεΐδης ‘son of Oeneus’, that is Tydeus, so Οἰνεΐδαο πάϊς ‘the child of Oeneus’ son’ is Diomedes, in apposition to ὄναρ: the evil dream is Diomedes himself standing over the sleeper. μῆτιν is ‘cunning’; διά with the accusative gives the cause, ‘through the cunning of Athena’.

sentences.t: τόφρα δ’ ἄρ’ ὃ τλήμων Ὀδυσεὺς λύε μώνυχας ἵππους,
sentences.l: And meanwhile enduring Odysseus was loosing the solid-hoofed horses,
sentences.i: Meanwhile enduring Odysseus was loosing the solid-hoofed horses,
sentences.n: The scene turns to Odysseus. τόφρα is ‘meanwhile’, ἄρα a light ‘so’, and ὃ τλήμων Ὀδυσεύς is ‘enduring Odysseus’ (τλήμων, the house rendering); ὃ before τλήμων is the article. λύε is the unaugmented imperfect of λύω ‘loose’, and μώνυχας ἵππους ‘solid-hoofed horses’ is the house phrase. The horses are those tied at 475.

sentences.t:
σὺν δ’ ἤειρεν ἱμᾶσι καὶ ἐξήλαυνεν ὁμίλου
τόξῳ ἐπιπλήσσων,
sentences.l:
and tied them together with straps and was driving them out of the throng,
striking them with the bow,
sentences.i: tied them together with straps and drove them out of the throng, striking them with his bow,
sentences.n: σὺν … ἤειρεν is tmesis, the verb συναείρω ‘tie together’ split in two, with ἱμᾶσι ‘straps’ (dative plural of ἱμάς). ἐξήλαυνεν ‘was driving out’ takes the genitive ὁμίλου ‘out of the throng’, the crowd of sleeping men. τόξῳ ἐπιπλήσσων is ‘striking at them with the bow’; the next unit says why a bow and not a whip.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὐ μάστιγα φαεινὴν
ποικίλου ἐκ δίφροιο νοήσατο χερσὶν ἑλέσθαι·
sentences.l:
since he had not thought to take the shining whip
from the intricate chariot in his hands;
sentences.i: since he had not thought to take the shining whip in his hands from the intricate chariot;
sentences.n: ἐπεί gives the reason for the bow. νοήσατο is the aorist middle of νοέω ‘perceive, think of’, followed by the infinitive ἑλέσθαι ‘to take’. μάστιγα φαεινήν is ‘a shining whip’, and ποικίλου ‘intricate’ (house) goes with δίφροιο ‘chariot’, the Thracians’ chariot. χερσίν ‘in his hands’ is the dative plural of χείρ. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ῥοίζησεν δ’ ἄρα πιφαύσκων Διομήδεϊ δίῳ.
sentences.l: and he whistled then, making it known to heavenly Diomedes.
sentences.i: and he whistled to signal to heavenly Diomedes.
sentences.n: ῥοίζησεν is the aorist of ῥοιζέω ‘make a whizzing or hissing sound’, here a whistle. πιφαύσκων ‘making known, signalling’ has no object in the Greek: the signal is understood from what follows, that it is time to leave. Διομήδεϊ is the epic dative of Διομήδης, and δίῳ ‘heavenly’ is the house rendering of δῖος.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ μερμήριζε μένων ὅ τι κύντατον ἕρδοι,
sentences.l: But he was pondering, staying where he was, what most dog-like thing he might do,
sentences.i: But he stayed where he was, pondering what was the most shameless thing he could do:
sentences.n: ὃ ‘he’ is Diomedes, and μένων ‘staying’ shows he had not moved. μερμήριζε is the imperfect of μερμηρίζω ‘ponder’, and ὅ τι ‘what’ with the optative ἕρδοι (from ῥέζω ‘do’) makes a deliberation. κύντατον is the superlative of κύων ‘dog’, ‘most dog-like’; the house line gives ‘shameless’ for the family (compare κύντερον ‘more shameless’ in the Odyssey), and here it means the boldest, most reckless deed, one that takes no thought of others. The next two units list his choices.

sentences.t:
ἢ ὅ γε δίφρον ἑλών, ὅθι ποικίλα τεύχε’ ἔκειτο,
ῥυμοῦ ἐξερύοι ἢ ἐκφέροι ὑψόσ’ ἀείρας,
sentences.l:
either he, taking the chariot where the intricate armour lay,
might drag it out by the pole, or carry it out, lifting it up high,
sentences.i: whether to take the chariot where the intricate armour lay and drag it out by the pole, or to lift it high and carry it out,
sentences.n: ἢ ὅ γε … ἢ ἐκφέροι … ἦ (506) lays out the choices: ‘either … or … or’. ἑλών is ‘having taken’, ὅθι ‘where’, and ποικίλα τεύχε’ ‘intricate armour’ (house), with ἔκειτο ‘lay’. δίφρον ‘chariot’ is the Thracian chariot with the armour in it. ῥυμοῦ is the genitive of ῥυμός ‘pole’, ‘by the pole’. ἐξερύοι and ἐκφέροι are optatives of ἐξερύω ‘drag out’ and ἐκφέρω ‘carry out’, and ὑψόσ’ ἀείρας ‘lifting it up high’.

sentences.t: ἦ ἔτι τῶν πλεόνων Θρῃκῶν ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο.
sentences.l: or still, of the more Thracians, take away the life.
sentences.i: or to take the lives of still more of the Thracians.
sentences.n: ἦ ‘or’ gives the last choice, and ἔτι ‘still’. ἀπὸ … ἕλοιτο is tmesis for ἀφέλοιτο ‘take away’, with θυμόν ‘life’ (as at 495) as object. τῶν πλεόνων Θρῃκῶν is ‘the more numerous Thracians’, genitive plural of Θρῇξ with the article; the sense is ‘yet more of the Thracians’.

sentences.t:
εἷος ὃ ταῦθ’ ὥρμαινε κατὰ φρένα, τόφρα δ’ Ἀθήνη
ἐγγύθεν ἱσταμένη προσέφη Διομήδεα δῖον·
sentences.l:
While he was pondering these things in his mind, meanwhile Athena,
standing near, addressed heavenly Diomedes:
sentences.i: While he was turning this over in his mind, Athena came and stood near and spoke to heavenly Diomedes:
sentences.n: εἷος is the form of ἧος ‘while’, and ὥρμαινε the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω ‘ponder, turn over’; τόφρα … ‘meanwhile’. ἐγγύθεν is ‘from near’ and ἱσταμένη ‘taking her stand’. προσέφη ‘addressed’ takes the accusative Διομήδεα, the epic accusative of Διομήδης, with δῖον ‘heavenly’. The edition prints no quotation marks; the speech starts with the next unit.

sentences.t:
νόστου δὴ μνῆσαι μεγαθύμου Τυδέος υἱὲ
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς,
sentences.l:
“Think now of your return, son of great-hearted Tydeus,
to the hollow ships,
sentences.i: “Think now of your return, son of great-hearted Tydeus, to the hollow ships,
sentences.n: Athena’s speech begins. μνῆσαι is the aorist middle imperative of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember, think of’, with the genitive νόστου ‘return’; δή is ‘now’. Τυδέος υἱέ is the vocative ‘son of Tydeus’, with μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted’ (house). In νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς the preposition stands after its noun (ἐπὶ νῆας), and γλαφυράς is ‘hollow’.

sentences.t: μὴ καὶ πεφοβημένος ἔλθῃς,
sentences.l: lest you even come, put to flight,
sentences.i: lest you even go back in flight,
sentences.n: μή with the aorist subjunctive ἔλθῃς gives a warning, ‘lest you come’. πεφοβημένος is the perfect passive participle of φοβέω ‘put to flight’, so ‘in flight’; καί is ‘even’: the return might turn into a rout. A second warning follows in the next unit.

sentences.t: μή πού τις καὶ Τρῶας ἐγείρῃσιν θεὸς ἄλλος.
sentences.l: lest perhaps some other god rouse the Trojans too.”
sentences.i: lest perhaps some other god rouse the Trojans too.”
sentences.n: μή πού τις … ἐγείρῃσιν is another warning, ‘lest perhaps some … rouse’; ἐγείρῃσιν is the epic subjunctive of ἐγείρω (-ῃσιν for -ῃ). καί is ‘too’, and θεὸς ἄλλος ‘another god’ means a god besides Athena; Apollo is the one who does so at 515–518. This ends Athena’s speech.

sentences.t: ὣς φάθ’, ὃ δὲ ξυνέηκε θεᾶς ὄπα φωνησάσης,
sentences.l: So she spoke, and he understood the voice of the goddess speaking,
sentences.i: So she spoke, and he understood the voice of the goddess who had spoken,
sentences.n: The same line stands at 2.182, where it is Odysseus who hears Athena; here the one who understands is Diomedes, and the English is kept the same. φάθ’ is ἔφατο, unaugmented. ξυνέηκε is the aorist of συνίημι ‘understand’, with the old spelling ξυν- and the epic ending -έηκε. φωνησάσης is the aorist participle agreeing with θεᾶς: ‘of the goddess who had spoken’.

sentences.t: καρπαλίμως δ’ ἵππων ἐπεβήσετο·
sentences.l: and swiftly he mounted the horses;
sentences.i: and swiftly he mounted the horses;
sentences.n: ἐπεβήσετο is the aorist middle of ἐπιβαίνω ‘mount’, here with the genitive ἵππων ‘the horses’: there is no chariot, so he gets up on a horse. καρπαλίμως ‘swiftly’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
κόψε δ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
τόξῳ·
sentences.l:
and struck them Odysseus
with the bow;
sentences.i: and Odysseus struck them with the bow;
sentences.n: The subject changes to Odysseus in the middle of the line. κόψε is the aorist of κόπτω ‘strike’, and τόξῳ ‘with the bow’ repeats 500: the bow still stands in for the whip.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἐπέτοντο θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: and they flew to the swift ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and they flew to the swift ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: τοί is the article used as a pronoun, ‘they’, the horses with their riders. ἐπέτοντο is the imperfect of πέτομαι ‘fly’, a picture of speed. θοάς ‘swift’ is the stock epithet of ships, and Ἀχαιῶν the genitive of ‘Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἀλαοσκοπιὴν εἶχ’ ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων
ὡς ἴδ’ Ἀθηναίην μετὰ Τυδέος υἱὸν ἕπουσαν·
sentences.l:
And no blind man’s watch kept silver-bowed Apollo
when he saw Athena going after the son of Tydeus;
sentences.i: And silver-bowed Apollo kept no blind man’s watch when he saw Athena following the son of Tydeus;
sentences.n: ἀλαοσκοπιήν is a rare noun, ‘a blind man’s watch’ (ἀλαός ‘blind’ + σκοπιή ‘lookout’), and οὐδ’ … εἶχ’ is ‘kept no’, so Apollo watched keenly; the Odyssey has the same phrase of Ares (8.285). ἀργυρότοξος ‘silver-bowed’ is the house rendering of Apollo’s epithet. ἴδ’ is ἴδε ‘saw’; μετά with the accusative is ‘after’, and ἕπουσαν ‘following’ agrees with Ἀθηναίην. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: τῇ κοτέων Τρώων κατεδύσετο πουλὺν ὅμιλον,
sentences.l: bearing a grudge against her, he went into the great throng of the Trojans,
sentences.i: and, holding a grudge against her, he went into the great throng of the Trojans,
sentences.n: τῇ is the dative of the article as a pronoun, ‘at her’, with κοτέων ‘bearing a grudge’ (κοτέω, as in the Odyssey). κατεδύσετο is the epic aorist middle of καταδύω ‘go down into, enter’, and Τρώων … πουλὺν ὅμιλον is ‘the great throng of the Trojans’, πουλύν the epic form of πολύν.

sentences.t:
ὦρσεν δὲ Θρῃκῶν βουληφόρον Ἱπποκόωντα
Ῥήσου ἀνεψιὸν ἐσθλόν·
sentences.l:
and he roused of the Thracians the counsel-bearer Hippocoon,
a good cousin of Rhesus;
sentences.i: and he roused Hippocoon, a counsellor of the Thracians, a good cousin of Rhesus;
sentences.n: ὦρσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, with Ἱπποκόωντα, the accusative of the name Hippocoon, as object. βουληφόρον ‘counsel-bearing’ means a counsellor (house rendering). Θρῃκῶν is the genitive plural ‘of the Thracians’, ἀνεψιόν ‘cousin’, ἐσθλόν ‘good’, and Ῥήσου the genitive of Rhesus. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐξ ὕπνου ἀνορούσας
ὡς ἴδε χῶρον ἐρῆμον, ὅθ’ ἕστασαν ὠκέες ἵπποι,
ἄνδράς τ’ ἀσπαίροντας ἐν ἀργαλέῃσι φονῇσιν,
sentences.l:
and he, from sleep having leapt up,
when he saw the place deserted, where had stood the swift horses,
and the men gasping in grievous slaughter,
sentences.i: He leapt up from sleep, and when he saw the deserted place where the swift horses had stood, and the men gasping in grievous slaughter,
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Hippocoon. ἀνορούσας is the aorist participle of ἀνορούω ‘spring up’, with ἐξ ὕπνου ‘from sleep’. The ὡς ἴδε clause (‘when he saw’) has two objects: χῶρον ἐρῆμον ‘the deserted place’ and ἄνδρας ἀσπαίροντας ‘men gasping’. ὅθ’ is ὅθι ‘where’, and ἕστασαν is a pluperfect used for ‘had stood’. φονῇσιν is the dative plural of φονή ‘slaughter’, and ἀργαλέος ‘grievous’ is the house rendering.

sentences.t: ᾤμωξέν τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα φίλον τ’ ὀνόμηνεν ἑταῖρον.
sentences.l: and he cried out then, and named his dear companion.
sentences.i: he cried out, and called his dear companion by name.
sentences.n: The main verbs are ᾤμωξεν (the aorist of οἰμώζω ‘cry out in grief’, with the particle τ’ after it) and ὀνόμηνεν (the aorist of ὀνομαίνω ‘name, call by name’). The companion is not named; it is presumably Rhesus, but the Greek does not say. ἄρ’ ἔπειτα is ‘then, after that’.

sentences.t:
Τρώων δὲ κλαγγή τε καὶ ἄσπετος ὦρτο κυδοιμὸς
θυνόντων ἄμυδις·
sentences.l:
And from the Trojans clamour and boundless uproar arose
as they rushed together;
sentences.i: Then a clamour went up from the Trojans, and a boundless uproar, as they rushed together;
sentences.n: Τρώων is the genitive ‘from the Trojans’, and θυνόντων ἄμυδις ‘as they rushed together’ is a genitive participle agreeing with it (θύνω ‘rush’). κλαγγή ‘clamour’, ἄσπετος ‘boundless’, κυδοιμός ‘uproar’ (the Odyssey’s ‘boundless clamour’ for the same adjective), and ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘arose’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
θηεῦντο δὲ μέρμερα ἔργα
ὅσσ’ ἄνδρες ῥέξαντες ἔβαν κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας.
sentences.l:
and they gazed at the baneful deeds,
all that the men had done before they went to the hollow ships.
sentences.i: and they gazed at the baneful deeds, all that the men had done before going off to the hollow ships.
sentences.n: θηεῦντο is the imperfect of θηέομαι ‘gaze at’; the Trojans are still the subject. μέρμερα ἔργα ‘baneful deeds’ is the house rendering (the origin of μέρμερος is uncertain). ὅσσ’ ‘all that’ goes with ῥέξαντες ‘having done’, and ἔβαν is the epic aorist ‘went’ of βαίνω. κοίλας ‘hollow’ goes with νῆας.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵκανον ὅθι σκοπὸν Ἕκτορος ἔκταν,
sentences.l: But when indeed they came to where Hector’s scout they had killed,
sentences.i: But when they came to the place where they had killed Hector’s scout,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘but they’ are Odysseus and Diomedes, back at the spot of the earlier killing. ὅτε δή ῥ’ is ‘when then’ (ῥ’ is ἄρα). ἵκανον is an epic past of ἱκάνω ‘come’, ὅθι ‘where’, and ἔκταν the short aorist of κτείνω, ‘they killed’. σκοπόν ‘scout’ is Dolon, who was killed earlier in this book; his name comes at 570.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ Ὀδυσεὺς μὲν ἔρυξε Διῒ φίλος ὠκέας ἵππους,
sentences.l: there Odysseus, dear to Zeus, held back the swift horses,
sentences.i: there Odysseus, dear to Zeus, held back the swift horses,
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ‘there’, ἔρυξε the aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, and ὠκέας ‘swift’. Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’ (house) is a stock epithet of Odysseus, and the edition prints the diaeresis on Διῒ.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδης δὲ χαμᾶζε θορὼν ἔναρα βροτόεντα
ἐν χείρεσσ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ τίθει, ἐπεβήσετο δ’ ἵππων·
sentences.l:
and the Tydeus’-son, to the ground leaping, the bloody spoils
into the hands of Odysseus put, and mounted the horses;
sentences.i: and the son of Tydeus leapt to the ground, put the bloody spoils into Odysseus’ hands, and mounted the horses;
sentences.n: Τυδεΐδης ‘the son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes. θορών is the aorist participle of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, and χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’. ἔναρα ‘spoils stripped from the slain’ are Dolon’s, which Odysseus had hung on a tamarisk earlier; βροτόεντα ‘bloody’. Ὀδυσῆϊ is the epic dative of Ὀδυσσεύς, and τίθει the imperfect of τίθημι ‘put’. ἐπεβήσετο δ’ ἵππων is ‘and mounted the horses’, as at 513. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
μάστιξεν δ’ ἵππους, τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς·
sentences.l:
and he whipped the horses, and the two, not unwilling, flew
to the hollow ships;
sentences.i: and he whipped the horses, and the pair flew, not unwilling, to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: μάστιξεν is the aorist of μαστίζω ‘whip’. In τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην the dual is used for the two horses: τώ is the dual article, ἀέκοντε the dual of ἀέκων ‘unwilling’, and πετέσθην the dual past of πέτομαι ‘fly’. The half-line recurs at 5.366, 5.768 and 8.45. νῆας ἔπι is ἐπὶ νῆας with the preposition after its noun. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: τῇ γὰρ φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ.
sentences.l: for thither it was dear to their spirit.
sentences.i: for it pleased their spirit to go that way.
sentences.n: τῇ is the adverb ‘thither, that way’, pointing to the ships. φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ is ‘was dear to the spirit’, so ‘it pleased the spirit’ in the English; ἔπλετο is a past form ‘was, had become’, and θυμῷ the dative of the heart. The Greek does not say whose heart; it fits the horses of the clause before.

sentences.t: Νέστωρ δὲ πρῶτος κτύπον ἄϊε φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l: And Nestor first heard the thud, and spoke:
sentences.i: Nestor was the first to hear the thud, and he spoke:
sentences.n: The scene shifts to the camp. Νέστωρ … πρῶτος is ‘Nestor first’; κτύπον ‘thud, beating’ is the sound of hooves. ἄϊε is the unaugmented past of ἀΐω ‘hear’, and φώνησεν the aorist of φωνέω ‘speak’, with τε ‘and’ joining the two. The edition prints no quotation marks; the speech starts with the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
ψεύσομαι, ἦ ἔτυμον ἐρέω;
sentences.l:
“O friends, leaders and lords of the Argives,
shall I speak falsely, or shall I say what is true?
sentences.i: “Friends, leaders and lords of the Argives: shall I be lying, or shall I say what is true?
sentences.n: Nestor addresses the chiefs; the line ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες also opens speeches at 2.79 and 9.17. ψεύσομαι is the future of ψεύδομαι ‘lie, speak falsely’ and ἐρέω the future of the verb ‘say’; both are deliberative, ‘shall I …?’, and ἔτυμον is ‘what is true’. The half-line is the Odyssey’s (4.140), and the English is shared.

sentences.t: κέλεται δέ με θυμός.
sentences.l: And my heart bids me speak.
sentences.i: But my heart urges me to speak.
sentences.n: κέλεται is the middle of κέλομαι ‘bid, urge’, and θυμός ‘heart’ is what urges him. No infinitive is given, and ‘to speak’ is supplied from the question before. The same words stand at Odyssey 4.140, and the English is shared.

sentences.t: ἵππων μ’ ὠκυπόδων ἀμφὶ κτύπος οὔατα βάλλει.
sentences.l: Of horses swift-footed the thud around strikes my ears.
sentences.i: The thud of swift-footed horses is beating around my ears.
sentences.n: ἵππων ὠκυπόδων ‘of swift-footed horses’ goes with κτύπος ‘thud’, as in 532. μ’ is the elided pronoun ‘me’ (με or μοι), so οὔατα βάλλει is ‘strikes my ears’; οὔατα is the epic plural of οὖς ‘ear’. ἀμφί is ‘around’, and the pronoun is rendered once, in ‘my ears’; and ὠκύποδες ‘swift-footed’ is the house rendering.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ δὴ Ὀδυσεύς τε καὶ ὃ κρατερὸς Διομήδης
ὧδ’ ἄφαρ ἐκ Τρώων ἐλασαίατο μώνυχας ἵππους·
sentences.l:
If only Odysseus and strong Diomedes
so quickly from the Trojans might drive off solid-hoofed horses;
sentences.i: If only Odysseus and strong Diomedes might drive solid-hoofed horses off from the Trojans, so, at once;
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ introduces a wish, with the aorist optative ἐλασαίατο (the epic third plural of the middle of ἐλαύνω ‘drive off’). ὧδ’ is ‘in this way, just so’ and ἄφαρ ‘at once’; ὃ before κρατερός is the article. κρατερὸς Διομήδης ‘strong Diomedes’ is the house phrase. Nestor does not know they are already doing it. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αἰνῶς δείδοικα κατὰ φρένα μή τι πάθωσιν
Ἀργείων οἳ ἄριστοι ὑπὸ Τρώων ὀρυμαγδοῦ.
sentences.l:
but dreadfully I fear in my mind lest they suffer something,
the best of the Argives, under the din of the Trojans.”
sentences.i: but I am dreadfully afraid in my mind that the best of the Argives may suffer some harm in the Trojans’ din.”
sentences.n: ἀλλά opposes a fear to the wish. δείδοικα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I fear’; αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’, κατὰ φρένα ‘in my mind’. μή τι πάθωσιν is μή with the aorist subjunctive, ‘lest they suffer something’, that is, some harm. Ἀργείων οἳ ἄριστοι ‘the best of the Argives’ means Odysseus and Diomedes; ὑπὸ … ὀρυμαγδοῦ ‘under the din’ marks the cause. This ends Nestor’s first speech.

sentences.t: οὔ πω πᾶν εἴρητο ἔπος ὅτ’ ἄρ’ ἤλυθον αὐτοί.
sentences.l: Not yet the whole word had been spoken, when they themselves came.
sentences.i: He had not yet finished speaking when they themselves arrived.
sentences.n: οὔ πω … ὅτ’ ἄρ’ is ‘not yet … when then’. εἴρητο is the pluperfect passive of the verb ‘say’, ‘had been said’; ἤλυθον is the epic past ‘came’; and αὐτοί ‘themselves’ are Odysseus and Diomedes. Compare Odyssey 16.11, which has the same first half.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ οἳ μὲν κατέβησαν ἐπὶ χθόνα, τοὶ δὲ χαρέντες
δεξιῇ ἠσπάζοντο ἔπεσσί τε μειλιχίοισι·
sentences.l:
and these then stepped down to the ground, and the others, rejoicing,
with the right hand greeted them, and with words gentle;
sentences.i: and these got down to the ground, and the others, glad to see them, greeted them with their right hands and with gentle words;
sentences.n: οἳ μέν … τοὶ δέ is ‘these … those’: Odysseus and Diomedes, and the chiefs waiting. κατέβησαν is the aorist of καταβαίνω ‘step down’ (from the horses); χαρέντες is the aorist passive participle ‘having rejoiced’. δεξιῇ is ‘with the right hand’ (the clasp); ἠσπάζοντο ‘greeted’; and μειλιχίοισι ‘gentle’ stands without its noun, ‘gentle words’. Odyssey 19.415 has the second half, with ‘hands’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: πρῶτος δ’ ἐξερέεινε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l: and first questioned them the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: And first the Gerenian horseman Nestor questioned them:
sentences.n: πρῶτος ‘first’ goes with ἐξερέεινε, the imperfect of ἐξερεείνω ‘question’. Γερήνιος ‘Gerenian’ and ἱππότα ‘horseman’ are Nestor’s stock epithets, and ἱππότα is the epic nominative. The edition prints no quotation marks; Nestor’s speech starts with the next unit.

sentences.t:
εἴπ’ ἄγε μ’ ὦ πολύαιν’ Ὀδυσεῦ μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν
ὅππως τοῦσδ’ ἵππους λάβετον καταδύντες ὅμιλον
Τρώων, ἦ τίς σφωε πόρεν θεὸς ἀντιβολήσας.
sentences.l:
“Come, tell me, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans,
how you two took these horses, having gone down into the throng
of the Trojans, or whether some god gave them to you two, having met you.
sentences.i: “Come, tell me, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans: how did you two get these horses, going down into the throng of the Trojans, or did some god meet you two and give them to you?
sentences.n: The first line stands also at 9.673, and its English is kept. εἴπ’ ἄγε is ‘come, tell’, and πολύαινος ‘much-praised’ is the house rendering. ὅππως is ὅπως ‘how’ in an indirect question; λάβετον is the dual of the aorist of λαμβάνω, ‘you two took’; and καταδύντες is ‘having gone down into’, with ὅμιλον ‘throng’. ἦ … gives the other possibility; σφωε is the dual accusative ‘you two’, πόρεν is ἔπορεν ‘gave’ (unaugmented), and ἀντιβολήσας ‘having met’.

sentences.t: αἰνῶς ἀκτίνεσσιν ἐοικότες ἠελίοιο.
sentences.l: Dreadfully like the rays of the sun.
sentences.i: Dreadfully like the rays of the sun.
sentences.n: αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’ is an intensifier here, as English says ‘awfully like’, and the English keeps ‘dreadfully’. ἐοικότες is the nominative plural of the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’. The noun last stood in the accusative (ἵππους, 545), so this is a loose exclamation about the horses rather than a clause bound to the question. ἀκτῖνες are ‘rays’, and ἠελίοιο is the epic genitive of ἠέλιος ‘sun’.

sentences.t:
αἰεὶ μὲν Τρώεσσ’ ἐπιμίσγομαι, οὐδέ τί φημι
μιμνάζειν παρὰ νηυσὶ γέρων περ ἐὼν πολεμιστής·
sentences.l:
Always I mingle with the Trojans, and in no way do I say
that I linger by the ships, though an old man, a warrior;
sentences.i: I am always mingling with the Trojans, and I deny that I linger by the ships, old though I am, and a warrior;
sentences.n: Nestor says he is always in the fight. ἐπιμίσγομαι is ‘mingle with’. οὐδέ τί φημι with an infinitive is ‘and I say … not at all’, that is, ‘I deny’; μιμνάζειν ‘linger’ is a rare verb. γέρων περ ἐὼν πολεμιστής is ‘though being an old man, a warrior’, with περ giving ‘though’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὔ πω τοίους ἵππους ἴδον οὐδὲ νόησα.
sentences.l: but never yet such horses have I seen or noticed.
sentences.i: but I have never yet seen or taken note of such horses.
sentences.n: τοίους ἵππους ‘such horses’ is the object of both verbs. ἴδον is the aorist of ‘see’ and νόησα the aorist of νοέω ‘perceive, take note of’. οὔ πω is ‘not yet’, so ‘never yet’.

sentences.t: ἀλλά τιν’ ὔμμ’ ὀΐω δόμεναι θεὸν ἀντιάσαντα·
sentences.l: but I think some god, having met you, gave them to you;
sentences.i: but I think some god met you and gave them to you;
sentences.n: ὔμμ’ is an elided epic ‘you’, either ὔμμι (dative, Attic ὑμῖν) or ὔμμε (accusative, Attic ὑμᾶς); the elision does not decide, and as accusative it would be the object of ἀντιάσαντα, as dative it would go with δόμεναι, with the sense ‘you’ either way. ὀΐω ‘I think’ takes the accusative θεόν with the infinitive δόμεναι (epic for δοῦναι), ‘that a god gave’, with ‘them’ (the horses) supplied. ἀντιάσαντα is the aorist participle of ἀντιάω ‘meet’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἀμφοτέρω γὰρ σφῶϊ φιλεῖ νεφεληγερέτα Ζεὺς
κούρη τ’ αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l:
for both of you loves cloud-gatherer Zeus,
and the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, gleaming-eyed Athena.”
sentences.i: for Zeus who gathers the clouds loves you both, and so does the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, gleaming-eyed Athena.”
sentences.n: ἀμφοτέρω σφῶϊ is the dual ‘you both’. φιλεῖ is singular, with the second subject κούρη … Ἀθήνη added after it. νεφεληγερέτα ‘cloud-gatherer’ (‘who gathers the clouds’), αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’, and γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ are all house renderings, and κούρη with a divine father is ‘daughter’. The first half-line is also 7.280. This ends Nestor’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is the present participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, and προσέφη ‘addressed’ the aorist of πρός + φημί. πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ is Odysseus’ stock epithet. The edition prints no quotation marks, and the speech starts with the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὦ Νέστορ Νηληϊάδη μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν
ῥεῖα θεός γ’ ἐθέλων καὶ ἀμείνονας ἠέ περ οἵδε
ἵππους δωρήσαιτ’, ἐπεὶ ἢ πολὺ φέρτεροί εἰσιν.
sentences.l:
“O Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans,
easily a god, if willing, even better horses than these
could give, since indeed they are much stronger.
sentences.i: “Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans, a god, if he wished, could easily give even better horses than these, since the gods are far stronger.
sentences.n: The address ὦ Νέστορ Νηληϊάδη μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν also opens Agamemnon’s speech at 10.87 and speeches at Odyssey 3.79 and 3.202, and its English is kept. ῥεῖα θεός γ’ ἐθέλων is also Odyssey 3.231, ‘easily a god, if willing’. δωρήσαιτ’ is the aorist optative of δωρέομαι ‘give’, a potential optative (‘could give’), and ἀμείνονας ἠέ περ οἵδε is ‘better than these’. The subject of εἰσιν is the gods, with the particle printed ἢ read as ἦ ‘truly’ and φέρτεροι ‘stronger’: they can do what men cannot.

sentences.t:
ἵπποι δ’ οἵδε γεραιὲ νεήλυδες οὓς ἐρεείνεις
Θρηΐκιοι·
sentences.l:
But these horses, old man, newcomers, which you ask about,
Thracian ones;
sentences.i: But these horses you are asking about, old man, are newcomers, and Thracian;
sentences.n: οἵδε ‘these’ points at the horses, and ἐρεείνεις is the present of ἐρεείνω ‘ask about’, picking up Nestor’s question. νεήλυδες ‘newcomers’ is the word used of the Thracians at 433 (the plural of νεήλυς), and Θρηΐκιοι is the adjective ‘Thracian’. The Greek has no verb: ‘are’ is supplied. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
τὸν δέ σφιν ἄνακτ’ ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης
ἔκτανε, πὰρ δ’ ἑτάρους δυοκαίδεκα πάντας ἀρίστους.
sentences.l:
and their lord good Diomedes
killed, and beside him twelve companions, all the best.
sentences.i: Good Diomedes killed their lord, and twelve companions beside him, all of them the best.
sentences.n: τὸν … ἄνακτα ‘that lord’ is Rhesus; σφιν is the dative ‘their’ (of possession). ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης is ‘good Diomedes’. ἔκτανε is the aorist of κτείνω; πάρ is παρά ‘beside’, used as an adverb. δυοκαίδεκα is ‘twelve’, and ἑτάρους ‘companions’ is the epic accusative plural of ἑταῖρος. The count of twelve picks up 488.

sentences.t:
τὸν τρισκαιδέκατον σκοπὸν εἵλομεν ἐγγύθι νηῶν,
τόν ῥα διοπτῆρα στρατοῦ ἔμμεναι ἡμετέροιο
Ἕκτωρ τε προέηκε καὶ ἄλλοι Τρῶες ἀγαυοί.
sentences.l:
as the thirteenth the scout we took near the ships,
whom indeed to be a spy of our army
Hector sent forth, and the other Trojans, noble ones.”
sentences.i: and as the thirteenth we caught a scout near the ships, whom Hector and the other noble Trojans sent out to spy on our army.”
sentences.n: Odysseus calls the scout the thirteenth, where line 495 called the king the thirteenth; the two counts do not agree, and the Greek is rendered as it stands. εἵλομεν is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take, catch’, and ἐγγύθι is ‘near’. διοπτῆρα ‘spy’ (one who looks through) is the predicate accusative with ἔμμεναι ‘to be’, giving the purpose: the scout (τόν) was sent to be a spy; στρατοῦ ἡμετέροιο is ‘of our army’. προέηκε is the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forth’, and ἀγαυοί ‘noble’ is the house rendering. This ends Odysseus’ speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν τάφροιο διήλασε μώνυχας ἵππους
καγχαλόων·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, across the ditch he drove the solid-hoofed horses,
exulting;
sentences.i: So saying, he drove the solid-hoofed horses across the ditch, exulting;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is ‘so saying’, closing the speech. διήλασε is the aorist of διελαύνω ‘drive through’, and the genitive τάφροιο ‘across the ditch’ is the ditch the Achaeans dug before the wall. καγχαλόων ‘exulting’ is the present participle of καγχαλάω. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ἅμα δ’ ἄλλοι ἴσαν χαίροντες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l: and with him the other Achaeans went, rejoicing.
sentences.i: and the other Achaeans went with him, rejoicing.
sentences.n: ἅμα δ’ is ‘and together with (him)’, with ἴσαν, the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’. χαίροντες ‘rejoicing’ agrees with Ἀχαιοί, whom the line names in the full form ἄλλοι … Ἀχαιοί ‘the other Achaeans’.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ὅτε Τυδεΐδεω κλισίην εὔτυκτον ἵκοντο,
sentences.l: And when to the well-made hut of the Tydeus’-son they came,
sentences.i: And when they reached the well-made hut of the son of Tydeus,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ὅτε is ‘and when they’, and ἵκοντο is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘arrive at’. Τυδεΐδεω is the epic genitive (-εω for -ου) of Τυδεΐδης. κλισίην ‘hut’ is the house rendering, and εὔτυκτον ‘well-made’ the house adjective (as in ‘a well-made lash’, 8.43).

sentences.t:
ἵππους μὲν κατέδησαν ἐϋτμήτοισιν ἱμᾶσι
φάτνῃ ἐφ’ ἱππείῃ, ὅθι περ Διομήδεος ἵπποι
ἕστασαν ὠκύποδες μελιηδέα πυρὸν ἔδοντες·
sentences.i: they tied the horses with well-cut straps at the horses’ manger, where Diomedes’ swift-footed horses stood eating honey-sweet wheat;
sentences.n: κατέδησαν is the aorist of καταδέω ‘tie up’, with ἐϋτμήτοισιν ‘well-cut’ (diaeresis as printed) and ἱμᾶσι ‘straps’. φάτνῃ ἐφ’ ἱππείῃ is ‘at the horses’ manger’ (ἱππείη ‘of horses’), and ὅθι περ ‘just where’. Διομήδεος is the epic genitive; ἕστασαν is a pluperfect used for ‘stood’; ὠκύποδες ‘swift-footed’ is the house rendering; πυρός is ‘wheat’ and ἔδοντες ‘eating’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
νηῒ δ’ ἐνὶ πρυμνῇ ἔναρα βροτόεντα Δόλωνος
θῆκ’ Ὀδυσεύς, ὄφρ’ ἱρὸν ἑτοιμασσαίατ’ Ἀθήνῃ.
sentences.l:
and in the stern of the ship the bloody spoils of Dolon
Odysseus placed, until they should prepare a holy offering for Athena.
sentences.i: And in the stern of the ship Odysseus put the bloody spoils of Dolon, until they could prepare a sacrifice for Athena.
sentences.n: Dolon is named here at last as the scout of 526. νηῒ is the dative of ναῦς (diaeresis as printed), ἐνὶ πρυμνῇ ‘in the stern’, and θῆκ’ is ἔθηκε ‘put’. ἱρόν is Ionic ἱερόν, a noun ‘sacred thing’, here the sacrifice due to Athena; ἑτοιμασσαίατ’ is the aorist optative of ἑτοιμάζω ‘prepare’ in the third plural, and ὄφρα with it is ‘until’ (or ‘so that’).

sentences.t:
αὐτοὶ δ’ ἱδρῶ πολλὸν ἀπενίζοντο θαλάσσῃ
ἐσβάντες κνήμας τε ἰδὲ λόφον ἀμφί τε μηρούς.
sentences.l:
and they themselves the much sweat washed off in the sea,
having stepped in, from the shins and the neck and about the thighs.
sentences.i: They themselves went into the sea and washed the great sweat off their shins, their necks and their thighs.
sentences.n: ἀπενίζοντο is the imperfect middle of ἀπονίζω ‘wash off’, with ἱδρῶ (the accusative of ἱδρώς ‘sweat’) as object, ‘washed the sweat off’. ἐσβάντες is the aorist participle of εἰσβαίνω (ἐσβαίνω) ‘step into’, and θαλάσσῃ ‘in the sea’ is a dative of place. κνήμας ‘shins’, λόφον ‘neck, nape’ and μηρούς ‘thighs’ name the parts washed. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only if the first syllable of ἀπενίζοντο, which opens the fourth foot, is read long (metrical lengthening).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί σφιν κῦμα θαλάσσης ἱδρῶ πολλὸν
νίψεν ἀπὸ χρωτὸς καὶ ἀνέψυχθεν φίλον ἦτορ,
sentences.l:
But when for them the wave of the sea the much sweat
had washed from the skin and their dear heart had cooled again,
sentences.i: But when the sea’s wave had washed the great sweat from their skin and their hearts were refreshed,
sentences.n: σφιν is ‘for them’. κῦμα θαλάσσης is ‘the wave of the sea’, the subject of νίψεν, the aorist of νίζω ‘wash’; ἀπὸ χρωτός is ‘from the skin’. ἀνέψυχθεν is the aorist passive of ἀναψύχω ‘cool again, refresh’, and φίλον ἦτορ ‘dear heart’ is its subject.

sentences.t: ἔς ῥ’ ἀσαμίνθους βάντες ἐϋξέστας λούσαντο.
sentences.l: into well-smoothed bathing-tubs they stepped, and washed.
sentences.i: they stepped into well-polished bathing-tubs and washed.
sentences.n: The same line stands at Odyssey 4.48, and the English is kept. ἔς ῥ’ is εἰς ἄρα, and ἀσαμίνθους is the accusative plural of ἀσάμινθος ‘bathing-tub’ (the Odyssey’s ‘bath’ for the singular). βάντες is the aorist participle of βαίνω ‘step’, ἐϋξέστας ‘well-polished’ (diaeresis as printed), and λούσαντο the aorist middle of λούω ‘wash’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ λοεσσαμένω καὶ ἀλειψαμένω λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ
δείπνῳ ἐφιζανέτην,
sentences.l:
And the two, having washed and anointed themselves richly with olive oil,
sat down to their meal,
sentences.i: The two of them, washed and richly anointed with olive oil, sat down to their meal,
sentences.n: τώ is the dual article, ‘the two’ (Diomedes and Odysseus); λοεσσαμένω and ἀλειψαμένω are dual aorist middle participles, ‘having washed (themselves)’ and ‘having anointed (themselves)’. λίπ’ is λίπα ‘richly’ and ἐλαίῳ ‘with olive oil’. ἐφιζανέτην is the dual imperfect of ἐφιζάνω ‘sit down at’, and δείπνῳ ‘meal’ is its dative. The dual here gives way to plurals in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἀπὸ δὲ κρητῆρος Ἀθήνῃ
πλείου ἀφυσσόμενοι λεῖβον μελιηδέα οἶνον.
sentences.l:
and from the mixing-bowl, to Athena,
drawing from the full one, they poured honey-sweet wine.
sentences.i: and drawing honey-sweet wine from a full mixing-bowl, they poured a libation to Athena.
sentences.n: The subject is now plural: ἀφυσσόμενοι ‘drawing’ and λεῖβον ‘poured a libation’ are plural after the duals. ἀπὸ … κρητῆρος is ‘from the mixing-bowl’, with πλείου ‘full’ agreeing with it, and μελιηδέα οἶνον ‘honey-sweet wine’. Ἀθήνῃ ‘to Athena’ is the dative of the goddess honoured, the same Athena who helped them.
